head: bc71f944c7aa3f212dee546ce218d96e62e25a8c
title: LLM post-hoc game review aimed at diagnosis
body:
Adds `mtg_ml.review`: an LLM reads played games, flags misplays and attributes each one to a cause in the setup. Docs: `docs/game-review.md`.

## How it works
- **record**: replay files plus `meta.review` (constructor args, agent specs, decklists, checkpoint iteration and games, training reward).
- **transcript**: every decision with a choice lists all offered options (the legal mask), the policy probability for each, the chosen option and the value estimate. Forced decisions show up as log lines. State is printed as diffs, with hidden information marked. About 25-45k tokens per game.
- **review**: backends `deepseek` (cheap first pass), `claude` (escalation, Opus 5.5 with server-side refusal fallback), and `prompt`/`file`, which let any agent (such as a Claude Code subagent) answer.
- **verify**: rebuilds the game at the decision with agent memory replayed, then runs paired rollouts over determinizations (common random numbers). Verdict is confirmed, refuted or inconclusive.
- **calibrate**: seeded faults with ground truth: hidden options (masking_gap), forced least-likely moves (sampling_noise), tampered life or power (engine_bug).

## First results (`v3-entity-500k` self-play; reviewer: Claude subagents through the prompt/file backend)
Calibration, 2 games: **6/7 seeded faults caught**. Life drift 2/2, power drift 1/1, forced blunders 2/2, blocking mask 1/2. The caught mask was flagged at confidence 0.45. The miss was a game where never blocking cost nothing visible.

Clean game s7, 4 findings, verified with 64 paired rollouts each:
| decision | claim | rollouts |
|---|---|---|
| d201 | at 3 life, Spawn double-blocks the already-blocked Serpent (p 0.82) and leaves Terror unblocked | **confirmed**, 0.00 → 0.77 |
| d145 | Nyxborn Hydra cast for X=0 with 5 lands (sampled, p 0.08) | **confirmed**, 0.02 → 0.22 |
| d133 | Familiar doesn't block Aberration (sampled, p 0.14) | inconclusive, +0.09 ± 0.08 |
| d140 | wrong land tapped for Spellbomb | **refuted**, −0.19 ± 0.08 |

d201 is a confident policy error. It may be an observation gap rather than undertraining: the next step is to check whether the features tell the policy that an attacker is already blocked.

## Reviewer comparison (8 fault-seeded `v3-entity-500k` self-play games, 27 seeded faults)

Every reviewer got the same transcripts. Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 ran as Claude Code subagents through the `prompt`/`file` backend (there is no Anthropic API key here); DeepSeek ran through its API.

| reviewer | caught | hidden blocks (8) | forced blunders (8) | life drift (8) | power drift (3) | blunders flagged under any cause | false engine/mask claims |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opus 5.5 | **22 / 27** | 5 | 6 | 8 | 3 | 7 / 8 | 0 |
| Sonnet 5.5 | 16 / 27 | 5 | 1 | 7 | 3 | 3 / 8 | 0 |
| deepseek-chat | 5 / 27 | 0 | 0 | 4 | 1 | 0 / 8 | 1 (+4 on clean games) |
| deepseek-reasoner | 14 / 27 (2 games: no answer) | 5 | 1 | 6 | 2 | 3 / 8 | 1 |

- **Opus** is the only reviewer that reliably finds sampled blunders and gives them the right cause.
- **Sonnet** matches Opus on engine and mask faults but mostly misses blunders, or files them under undertraining.
- **deepseek-chat** should not be used. On clean games it reported engine bugs that are correct rules: the ward trigger stacking above Cast Down, repeated Krark-Clan Shaman activations, an indestructible Bridge surviving Cleansing Wildfire, and blocked damage it misread as going through. It labels almost every sampled move as reward shaping, and it called the Jund Wildfire deck's normal play, Cleansing Wildfire on its own Bridge, a misplay.
- **deepseek-reasoner** runs with a 64k token cap, because at 8k and 32k its reasoning used up the budget and left no answer. Even at 64k, 2 of the 8 games came back with no answer (65,536 completion tokens, all reasoning), at about 10 minutes per game. On the 6 games it did answer, it caught 14 of 21 faults, as many hidden blocks as Opus (5 of 6 there), but almost no blunders. It made one false engine claim: Cleansing Wildfire on an indestructible Bridge. A cheap first pass for engine and mask problems if the empty answers are retried.

Recommendation: review with Opus 5.5 and verify every "B was better" claim with rollouts. Sonnet 5.5 is a cheaper first pass for engine and mask problems only.

## Tests
`tests/test_review.py`: transcript, chunking, reply parsing, mask fault, tamper and scoring, rebuild fidelity over a whole game, paired rollouts (same option gives a diff of exactly 0), and invalid options. No network.

head: 945d42f6d1f4530f739af5b2e2aa5b15a018a55d
title: Docs: representation plan for scaling to the Pauper meta
body:
Plan doc: `docs/representation-plan.md`. Docs only, no code or test changes.

Follows the r4-control game review (PR #31 handoff). Hand-written feature tokens per gap don't scale to ~25 decks, so:

1. Feature set 4, rules-level gaps only (combat relations, incoming damage, X, colours).
2. Indistinguishability audit: options with identical features but different successor states, reported per 1k decisions.
3. Simulated option previews (state delta after the option) on an O(1) cloneable Rust `Game`.
4. Entity tokens derived from `cards.toml` ability, trigger and cost shapes; hand cards as entities.
5. Relation table (blocks, targets, attached_to, x_of) read by entity attention.

head: ff4be530e0a45822eb500cc89139918681e35641
title: Feature set 4: combat relations, incoming damage, X and colour previews
body:
Step 1 of the representation plan: **feature set 4**, the rules-level observation gaps that the r4-control game review found (handoff `docs/handoff-2026-10-07-feature-set-4.md` on PR #31, P1 to P3 without Delver and P4). `encode.FEATURES = 4`, `FEATURE_VERSIONS = (1, 2, 3, 4)`. Everything new is gated on `features >= 4` and implemented in both engines. No rules change, and the golden digests are untouched.

## Sets 1 to 3 unchanged
The first commit adds `tests/data/features_v3_digests.json`, recorded with the code before set 4. It covers sets 2 and 3 on 18 random-play games: all three matchups, pre- and postboard. Each digest includes featurize, both seats' state features, entities with their index, and every option preview. `test_feature_sets_2_and_3_are_unchanged` checks it on both engines; it passes after the change. The set-1 digest test also passes.

## New tokens
**Combat (P1).** Attacker entities:
- `e:attack_slot:{j}`: declaration order.
- `e:blocked` / `e:unblocked`.
- `e:blockers>=k`, `e:block_power>=k`.
- `e:block_lethal`: the blockers' power or deathtouch destroys it.

Blocker entities:
- `e:blocking:slot:{j}`: the slot of the attacker it blocks.
- `e:blocking:name:`, `e:blocking:power>=k`, `e:blocking:toughness>=k`: that attacker's name, power and toughness.
- `e:blocking:kills` / `e:blocking:dies`: the result one on one.

`declare_blocker` previews:
- `pv:attacker_already_blocked`.
- `pv:attacker_dies`: existing blockers plus this one, with deathtouch.
- `pv:blocker_dies`.
- `pv:unblocked_damage_left>=k`.
- `pv:lethal_left`.

**Incoming damage (P2).**
- `{side}:attacking_power>=k`, `{side}:unblocked_power>=k`.
- `{side}:incoming_lethal`.
- `{defender}:life_after_unblocked>=k`: the optional thermometer from the handoff.

**choose_x (P3).**
- `pv:x>=k`, `pv:x_is_max`.
- X-inclusive `pv:mana_left_after:{k}` / `pv:colors_left:{C}`, from `_item_cost` with this X.
- `pv:enters_power>=k` for `etb_x_counters`.
- Each X option points at the stack item, through `option_object_ids` in both engines.

**Colours (P3).**
- State: `self:sources:{C}>=k`, `self:hand_needs:{C}`, `self:hand_missing:{C}`.
- Entities: `e:produces:{C}`.
- Land plays and `('search', card)` options: `pv:adds_color:{C}`, `pv:adds_missing_color`.
- `pay_mana` options: `pv:colors_left:{C}` after paying this unit. For this, both engines keep the pending payment in `Game.paying` / `State.paying`, which is read only by the preview.

Details and exact definitions are in `docs/features.md`, section "Feature set 4".

## Blocker -> attacker relation: tokens, not an entity pointer
Entity tokens are hashed into the state embedding. A true entity-to-entity pointer is a new input kind for the model: `Batch` structure, the native batcher, the inference server, and new weights. That is step 5 of the plan (relation table plus entity attention) and a different component.

This PR uses a slot pair instead: `e:attack_slot:{j}` on the attacker and `e:blocking:slot:{j}` on the blocker. The pair is the identity link that an attention layer can match. The attacker's name and P/T tokens on the blocker give a model without attention the content. A `declare_blocker` option already points at both the blocker and the attacker entity, so the new `e:blocked` / `e:unblocked` flags plus the previews are what separate two same-name attackers.

## Fixtures
`tests/data/feature_fixtures.json` (7.6 KB) stores 12 review decisions as constructor args plus action prefixes; the 50 MB replays are not copied. They are rebuilt by stepping, and the option labels are checked. The tests run on both engines:
- **Blocks:** at s1000 d153, s1035 d102, s1047 d229, s1047 d279 and s1010 d359, the two candidate block options have different signatures in set 4. A signature is the option's hashed tokens plus the token sets of the entities it points at. At the four same-name cases the signatures are identical in set 3. At s1010 d359, `pv:attacker_dies` is absent on the 3-power block of the 6/7. At s1000 d153, `pv:lethal_left` marks stacking on the blocked Terror.
- **Incoming damage:** `opponent:incoming_lethal` is set at s1000 d153 and s1049 d306.
- **s1011 d216 does not match the handoff.** The handoff cites it as an `incoming_lethal` fixture, but it is 12 + 4 = 16 unblocked against 18 life, which is not lethal. The test asserts `attacking_power>=15`, `unblocked_power>=15` and `self:life_after_unblocked>=2` (not `>=3`), and asserts that `incoming_lethal` is absent.
- **X and colours:** s1003 d250 checks X previews and the pointer, s1008 d333 checks payment colours, and s1033 d60 / s1048 d71 check the colours of basic-land searches.

## Tests
- `make lint`: clean.
- `make test`: 736 passed, 12 skipped, native built.
- `make difftest`: 2000/2000 games identical.
- `cargo test --no-default-features`: ok.
- `test_entity_and_preview_strings_identical` now compares state, entity and preview strings in set 3 and set 4 over 12 games of all three matchups. It also asserts that each of the 30 set-4 token families was seen at least once.
- `test_rl` expected `FEATURES == 4`. The "unknown version" check moved to `features=5`.

**Cost:** native `featurize_flat` is about 10-25% slower per decision with set 4 (12 to 48 µs/decision across runs on a busy M-series Mac, so the measurement is noisy).

## Blind-spot audit (PR #34's `mtg_ml.audit`, native engine, bot vs bot)
I ran it from a temporary copy of `mtg_ml/audit.py`; this PR does not include it.

| matchup, games | set 3 blind / 1k decisions | set 4 |
|---|---|---|
| jund_blue, 1000 | 1.853 (declare_blocker 80.1, target 3.6, priority 0.26) | **0.0** (every kind, also 0 identical-option groups) |
| jund_madness, 500 | 0.441 | **0.0** |
| blue_madness, 500 | 0.991 | **0.0** |

Set 4 also clears the priority and target cases from the audit. Two Spawn mana abilities on Spawns blocking different attackers are now told apart, and so is removal aimed at one of two same-name attackers where one is blocked. Both come from the blocker / attacker entity tokens.

## Not done here
- `tools/feature_collisions.py` (handoff P0) is replaced by PR #34's `mtg_ml.audit`, whose numbers are above.
- Delver reveal and P4 are out of scope.
- A fine-tune of r4-control with `--features 4` is the follow-up: the new rows start untrained.

head: 66e57babe0d9d989e729253ea23d4f5c8c115d15
title: Indistinguishability audit: find observation blind spots mechanically
body:
Step 2 of the representation plan (`docs/representation-plan.md` on `claude/representation-plan`): `python -m mtg_ml.audit` finds **blind spots**, decisions where two options get exactly the same network input but lead to different games.

## How it works

- **Grouping**: at each audited decision, options are grouped by their featurization in the decider's feature set (`rl.features.featurize`, so both engines and any set): hashed option tokens plus, for each entity pointer, the token bag of the entity it points at. The model is permutation-invariant over entities and pointers, so nothing else separates two options.
- **Check**: for every group of 2+, fork (`Game.fork`), step each option, compare `audit.canonical_view` of the decider: `view.observe` (no opponent hand, no library order) plus blocked attackers and the next decision if it is the decider's, with object ids replaced by Weisfeiler-Lehman labels over blocks / attached-to / targets. Interchangeable objects give equal views, while "two blockers on one Terror" and "one on each" differ. Differing views mean a blind spot.
- **Report**: blind spots per 1k decisions, by decision kind, seat and card; examples with seed, decision index, option keys/labels and the action prefix (`audit.rebuild(example)`); JSON `"format": 1` via `--out`, plus a text summary. `--agents` takes bots, random or checkpoints (each in its recorded feature set), `--features N` overrides (set 4 works as soon as it is in `FEATURE_VERSIONS`), `--sample-frac` samples decisions.

## Baselines (Apple M3, native engine, jund_blue)

| agents | set | games | blind / 1k | declare_blocker (blind / 1k of that kind) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| bot, bot | 1 | 1000 | 4.23 | 80.1 (plus pay_mana 16.9, target 12.6) |
| bot, bot | 2 | 1000 | 1.85 | 80.1 |
| bot, bot | 3 | 1000 | 1.85 | 80.1 (target 3.6, priority 0.26) |
| r4-control v07714 self-play, sampled | 3 | 400 | 2.19 | 88.7 |
| r4-control v07714 self-play, greedy | 3 | 200 | 2.80 | 114.5 |

Every set-3 blind spot is a combat relation: same-name attackers where one is already blocked (handoff P1), Eldrazi Spawns sacrificed for mana while blocking different attackers, removal on one of two same-name attackers. Set 1's extra `pay_mana` cases are bridges targeted by Cleansing Wildfire; set 2's `e:targeted_by` closed them, and the audit shows that. Bots, other matchups: jund_madness 0.28 / 1k, blue_madness 0.91 / 1k. Python and Rust engines give identical reports (checked on 30 games).

Runtime: native ~0.05 s per 1k decisions including bot play, Python ~0.36 s; with model agents the network dominates (~0.6 s per 1k).

## Tests

`tests/test_audit.py` (added to `ENGINE_MODULES`, runs on both engines, <1 s): two same-name attackers, one blocked, are a blind spot in set 3; the third blocker, with each attacker blocked by one identical Shaman, is not flagged in any set; canonical view and signature checks; a `run` / CLI smoke test with `rebuild` of every example. No engine or feature changes, so goldens and digests are unchanged.

Docs: `docs/audit.md`.

head: 76fd72d7d9bb088d81527541550591be8703ccd5
title: Feature set 5: card-shape entity tokens and hand cards as entities
body:
Step 4 of the representation plan (PR #32, `docs/representation-plan.md`): cards described by what they do, and the decider's hand cards as entities. **Feature set 5.**

**Stacked on feature set 4 (PR #33).** The base is `claude/feature-set-4` (head 759358e), so this diff shows only set 5. `FEATURES = 5`, `FEATURE_VERSIONS = (1, 2, 3, 4, 5)`. The repo squash-merges, so once #33 lands, rebase with `rebase --onto origin/HEAD <merge-base with origin/claude/feature-set-4>` and set the base back to the default branch. `docs/features.md` will conflict trivially with #34.

## What set 5 adds

- **Shape tokens from the card spec** (`cards.card_shape`, `native/src/cards.rs::card_shape`). Both engines compute them once per card, face and token when cards.toml loads; `mtg_ml_native.card_shapes()` exposes the native ones. They cover:
  - mana value (`e:mv>=k`), colours, and cost shapes (`e:cost:flashback|escape|madness|bestow|plot|overload|alternative|sac_lands|additional_sac|additional_discard|reduction:*|x`);
  - spell targets and ops (`e:spell:target:*`, `e:spell:op:*`);
  - per ability: zone, mana colours, activation mana value, tap / sacrifice / discard / exile costs, X, sorcery speed, targets and ops (`e:ab:*`);
  - per trigger: event, condition and ops (`e:trig:*`);
  - each op's amount as a thermometer (`:n>=k`), and context-free copies `e:op:*` / `e:target:*`, so a burn spell and a damage ability share their op.
- **Where the shape tokens go:**
  - a permanent gets its current face's shape;
  - a spell on the stack gets its card's shape;
  - every stack item gets `e:res:op:*` for the ops it will resolve.

  `e:name` stays, so learned card identities carry over.
- **Hand entities**: the decider's own hand, after the permanents and the stack. Each card gets `e:zone:hand`, its name, its printed types, keywords and P/T, its shape, and `e:castable` when the decider is at priority with an option to cast it from hand. The opponent's hand is never shown (its size stays a state feature).
- **Option pointers**: cast, play-land and plot options point at their hand entity (`option_object_ids(option, game, kind, features)`, gated on `features >= 5`, both engines).
- **Spec fields** are split into `SHAPE_*_FIELDS` and `NON_SHAPE_*_FIELDS` per level (card, ability, trigger). An unknown field or op fails to load with a message that names what to add in both engines, so new decks cannot silently skip `card_shape`.

Full token tables are in `docs/features.md`, section "Card shapes and hand entities (set 5)".

## Invariants

- Sets 1-4 are byte-identical. Set 4's own digest test covers sets 2 and 3. This PR adds `tests/data/features_v4_digests.json`, recorded with the set-4 code on the same 18 games, with both engines agreeing. The games use the decks pinned in `tests/data/feature_decks.json` (`pinned_game_args`, from #33), so sideboard and deck changes cannot move the digests; `test_feature_set_4_is_unchanged` checks it. The set-1 digest test also still passes.
- Every card-spec field is classified as shape or non-shape in both engines (`SHAPE_*_FIELDS` / `NON_SHAPE_*_FIELDS` in `cards.py` and `native/src/cards.rs`). An unknown field fails to load in either engine with an error naming those lists and both files; `test_spec_field_sets_identical` checks the lists match.
- Both engines produce identical output. `test_entity_and_preview_strings_identical` now covers sets 3 to 5, both seats' entities and the option pointer ids. `test_card_shapes_identical` compares every card's shape.
- Generalization at the input level:
  - `test_set_5_cards_that_work_alike_share_every_token_but_name_and_type`: Swamp and Vault of Whispers, and Brainstorm and Ponder.
  - `test_an_unseen_card_gets_the_shape_of_the_cards_it_plays_like`: a card spec outside the pool gets exactly Lightning Bolt's shape.
- Model: no constants changed. Entities per sample are dynamic. `MAX_ENTITIES = 64` truncates permanents, then the stack, then the hand. Old checkpoints load unchanged, because the feature set travels with the model.

## Changed test expectations

- `test_featurize_one_entry_per_legal_option`: at the opening mulligan, set 5 has 7 hand entities, so the check now looks only at the global part, which equals set 4's state.
- `test_feature_set_version_travels_with_the_model`: the latest set is now 5, and the unknown-version check uses 6.
- `test_entity_and_preview_strings_identical` (from set 4): loops over `FEATURE_VERSIONS[2:]` instead of `(3, FEATURES)`, compares both seats' entities, and compares option pointer ids.

head: eacb169b0a73b95fe9597a30162e25a489e76de3
title: Game.copy(): cheap exact game copies in both engines (representation plan step 3a)
body:
Step 3a of the representation plan: cheap, exact game copies in both engines, the infrastructure for simulated option previews (and for search, if it is tried again).

## What changed

- **`Game.copy()` / `NativeGame.copy()`**: an independent game in exactly the same state (object ids, RNG state, log, actions) that continues identically.
- **`fork()` now calls `copy()`**; `fork(replay=True)` is the old rebuild from constructor args + action history.
- Rust: `State` is `Clone` (constructor `Args` and the snapshot behind `Rc`); `PyGame.copy()`, `set_snapshots()`, `adopt_snapshot()`, `has_snapshot`. Finished games recycle their coroutine stack (thread-local pool of 64).
- Python: hand-written structured state copy (`game._copy_state`, ~20x faster than `copy.deepcopy`); card definitions and `ManaCost` are shared (`__deepcopy__` returns self).

## Why it is not a plain clone

Both engines are coroutines (a Python generator, a `corosensei` stack in Rust), and a suspended coroutine cannot be copied. So `copy()` restores a **snapshot of the data state taken at the start of the current step** (where the coroutine holds nothing but "which step, skip the draw?") and replays only the actions since that step began (median 1 in the benchmark, max 33). A copy costs roughly the same at decision 50 or 400.

- Only a game that has been copied takes snapshots. Its first `copy()` replays the whole history once, then turns snapshots on. A copy shares its parent's snapshot until its next step and takes none of its own unless it is copied too, so previews and playouts that are never copied pay nothing.
- Edits outside `step()` (native: every `PyGame::mutate`, meaning `set_card_def`, `add_card`, RNG `setstate`, etc.; Python: `view.determinize`, `add_card`) drop the snapshot. Until the next step, copying an edited game falls back to a replay, which drops the edits just as the old `fork()` did. From the next step on, copies keep them. Direct attribute writes on the Python engine are not tracked.

## Benchmark

`python tools/bench_copy.py --engine {python,native} --games 40`, scripted-bot games, median per copy, Apple M3 (16 GB) **under heavy load** (seven other agent sessions, load ~60), so the numbers are noisy:

| decision | Python replay | Python copy | speed-up | Rust replay | Rust copy | speed-up |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 50 | 2.36 ms | 0.17 ms | 14x | 0.139 ms | 0.019 ms | 7x |
| 200 | 8.78 ms | 0.24 ms | 37x | 0.458 ms | 0.022 ms | 21x |
| 400 | 20.3 ms | 0.25 ms | 83x | 1.032 ms | 0.018 ms | 58x |

Snapshot price, only paid by a game that has been copied, per decision under random play: Rust 5.9 to 6.5 µs, Python 92 to 261 µs.

## Tests

- `tests/test_copy.py` (in `ENGINE_MODULES`, so it runs on both engines): copy vs replay fork across 3 matchups, many seeds and random decision points, comparing difftest `snapshot()` (decision, observe, state features, featurize v1 and the default version, event hashes, full state) plus `outcome()` (log, full RNG state, actions) at every step of a random continuation. Also covers independence (mutating or finishing a copy leaves the original alone), copies of copies, scenario games with a setup callback and a non-untap start step, and determinized games. A larger version is marked `@slow`.
- `mtg_ml.difftest`'s fork check now also steps the copies once and compares `copy()` with `fork(replay=True)` inside each engine.
- No golden digests changed, and no test assertions changed.

## Callers whose behaviour could change

- `fork()` callers (`view.determinize` on Python, `NativeGame.determinize`, difftest, tests) get a copy instead of a replay. The two are the same unless the game was edited outside `step()`. Then a copy keeps edits made before the current step began, while a replay never kept any. `SearchBot` playouts are not copied again, so nothing changes for them.
- A game that has been copied once keeps taking step-start snapshots (see the price above).

head: b6d63ef4e185b08b5f567c26eaf5f3248e0070e1
title: Feature set 6: simulated option previews
body:
Step 3b of the representation plan (`docs/representation-plan.md`, "Simulated option previews"): **feature set 6**. Stacked on #35 (set 5, card shapes; this PR's base) and #36 (`Game.copy`, merged in).

## What it does

For every option of every decision, `pv:sim:*` option tokens from a simulation: copy the game, take the option, advance while that needs no hidden information and no choice of the opponent, featurize the change the decider can observe. The set 2-5 previews stay. `FEATURES = 6`, `FEATURE_VERSIONS = (1, ..., 6)`, everything gated on `features >= 6`; option tokens only, so the model is unchanged.

**Stops** (`pv:sim:stop:*`): `own_decision`, `opponent_decision`, `game_over` (+ `pv:sim:won/lost/draw_game`), `hidden_info` (only this token), `step_cap` (64 steps); `pv:sim:skipped` above 32 options or without a step-start snapshot (mulligans).

- The opponent's decisions are taken only when forced: one option and a kind whose options are public (target, pay_mana, sacrifice, exile_from_graveyard, order_triggers, declare_attacker/blocker, assign_damage, choose_x). On a simulation copy (`Game.sim_viewer`) the opponent's single-option decisions are asked instead of auto-taken.
- **Priority always stops**, the decider's or the opponent's, before its options are listed: the opponent's would read its hand. Consequence: the decider's own spell does not resolve in its previews (the opponent gets priority first); passing as the second player does show the stack resolving (the opponent's Bolt killing your creature, or the life loss). Combat damage is not simulated (priority after blocks); set 4's block previews keep covering it.
- **Hidden information** = a library shuffled (`Game.shuffles`), a card leaving / entering / moving in a library, or a library card the decider did not know being looked at. Revealing a card the decider already knows (Delver) is not hidden.

**Delta tokens**: next decision (`pv:sim:next:{self,opponent}:{kind}`), new turn / step, life per side (signed thermometer), creatures lost per side (count, summed power, per-creature power tiers), creatures and permanents gained / lost, tapped / untapped, damage marked, hand / graveyard / exile / library size changes per side (counts only), stack size, the decider's mana left and colours, lethal flags at the stop and gained / lost (`lethal_on_board`, `evasive_lethal_on_board`, `incoming_lethal`). The engine has no poison counters, so no poison token. Full table in `docs/features.md`.

## If the opponent passes (`pv:simp:*`)

Every option also gets the same token families under `pv:simp:`, from a second simulation that assumes the opponent passes (`Game.sim_assume_pass`, both engines). At the opponent's priority the engine takes its pass, which is always legal, without listing its options; nothing else it could do is considered and nothing about its hand is read. All other stops are unchanged: the decider's next decision (own priority included), non-forced opponent decisions, hidden information, game over, the step cap. `pv:sim:` stays exactly as it was (the "they may respond" view).

- Own Lightning Bolt on a creature: `pv:simp:opponent:creatures_lost>=1`. Own Counterspell: both spells leave the stack. A creature spell: `pv:simp:self:creatures_gained`, `power_gained`. The attacker passing in the declare-blockers step: combat damage dealt, `pv:simp:won` on lethal.
- The second simulation runs only when the first stopped at the opponent's priority (25-26% of options in random play). Otherwise it would be the same simulation, so the first result is **repeated under `pv:simp:`**. I picked that over a single `pv:simp:same` token so each prefix always means the same thing (for example `pv:simp:self:creatures_lost` always means "lost if the opponent does nothing") and the network need not combine the two families. The repeat costs only token hashing. `pv:sim:skipped` comes with `pv:simp:skipped`.

## Hidden-information guarantee

The summaries read public objects, zone sizes, the decider's mana and flags; the simulation never continues past a library touch and never lists the opponent's options. `tests/test_sim_previews.py::test_hidden_cards_never_change_sim_tokens` (both engines, all three matchups): pairs of games from the same public position whose hidden cards differ (opponent's hand + library split and order; in half of the runs also the decider's library order) are played with the same choices while the decider's observation stays equal, and every option's previews must be equal at every decider decision, `pv:sim:` and `pv:simp:` alike (the test also requires some `pv:simp:` to differ from `pv:sim:`, so the second simulation is exercised). Disabling `sim_viewer` makes it fail on every matchup. Plus targeted tests: Counterspell vs a land in the opponent's hand gives equal `pv:sim:` and `pv:simp:` (the Bolt resolves in both `pv:simp:`); a draw stops the simulation.

## Engine changes (both engines)

- `Game.sim_viewer` (ask the other player's single-option decisions; stop at any priority) and `Game.shuffles`. Never set on a played game; golden digests unchanged.
- Rust: a suspended game is dropped by resuming `ask` with an abort index that returns `Stop::Abort` through ordinary returns instead of unwinding the coroutine: ~4x cheaper drop, which made per-option copies affordable (step + drop of a copy 20 -> 4.4 µs measured under load).
- `features::featurize` takes the precomputed per-option sim hashes; `PyGame.featurize / featurize_flat / option_preview` are `&mut` (they copy), new `option_previews` and `edited`. The Python wrapper makes sure a never-copied game has a snapshot before set 6 (`NativeGame._sim_ready`).

## Cost

`python tools/bench_sim.py` (random play, all matchups, 4048 decisions, 2.8 options per decision, second simulation on 25-26% of options; Apple M3 laptop shared with other agents, load ~7). `featurize_flat` per decision:

| | set 5 | set 6 | added |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Rust mean | 15.2 µs | 38.5 µs | +23.3 µs (**2.5x**) |
| Rust median | 14.9 µs | 32.4 µs | +17.5 µs (2.2x) |
| Python mean | 223 µs | 1480 µs | +1257 µs (6.6x) |

Before `pv:simp:` the same Rust benchmark gave 14.6 -> 32.4 µs (2.2x mean), so the second simulation adds about 5.5 µs per decision. Each simulation costs about 6 µs in Rust, two thirds of it the copy (state clone, coroutine restart, replay of the ~1.7 actions since the step began) and its drop. This is above the ~2x target on the mean. Games featurized in set 6 take a snapshot at every step start (`Game.copy` semantics), included in the step time (Rust step mean 5.9 µs).

## Blind-spot audit (`mtg_ml/audit.py` from #34, not committed)

| matchup (bots, 50 games, native) | decisions | set 5 blind/1k | set 6 blind/1k |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| jund_blue | 14633 | 0 | 0 |
| jund_madness | 11413 | 0 | 0 |
| blue_madness | 8363 | 0 | 0 |

Random play (30 games per matchup): also 0 and 0; set 5 left one colliding group in total (truly equivalent, equal sim tokens). Set 5's hand entities and pointers already separate the options, so the audit cannot show set 6's gain (it adds consequences of options, which the audit does not score). Reverse check: of 311 option groups whose successors the audit calls equivalent (random play, 8 games per matchup), 2 get different sim tokens, both momentary public differences the audit's longer successor washes out (which land stays untapped until the next untap; a damage split before cleanup). Before restricting the reveal check to the decider's knowledge, Delver's "reveal / don't reveal" made 22 such false splits.

## Tests

- `tests/data/features_v5_digests.json` + `test_feature_set_5_is_unchanged` (recorded before any set-6 code, on the pinned decks): sets 1-5 byte-identical on both engines.
- `tests/test_sim_previews.py` (in `ENGINE_MODULES`): `pv:simp:` tests (own Bolt kills, own Counterspell counters, own creature resolves, the attacker's pass wins on lethal combat damage, `pv:simp:` repeats `pv:sim:` when no opponent priority comes up), hidden-information property test, stop reasons, creature death on resolution, different outcomes of the same option, lethal combat -> `pv:sim:lost`, mana / colours after payment, skips, no sim tokens before set 6.
- `make difftest`: 2000 of 2000 games identical (run in three chunks, with `pv:simp:`). `test_entity_and_preview_strings_identical` covers sets 3-6 (`pv:simp:` too), `option_previews` too, and checks that the stop reasons and common deltas occur. `test_identical_errors_in_both_engines_are_reported` patches `step` on the class (an instance attribute would be carried into set 6's copies). `test_rl`: `FEATURES == 6`.

Test changes that alter expected behaviour: `FEATURES == 6` in `test_rl`, and the difftest error-injection test's patching method; no golden digest changed.

head: 9a6cd48b9cf3d27f201a35c2a6f9ed3161b238c8
title: Bound combat damage divisions; split oversized inference requests (r6 crash)
body:
Fixes the r6 crash `ValueError: request of 18951046 ints does not fit (ServerConfig.request_ints = 2097152)` (h256, iter 134; h128: 2144403 ints at iter 183). Based on `claude/r6-integration` (#45); merge after #45.

## Root cause
Not a batch of many games and not the set-6 sim tokens (those are capped at 32 options). It was a single ASSIGN_DAMAGE decision: an attacker blocked by several creatures was offered every composition of its power over the blockers (+ the player with trample), C(pw + slots - 1, slots - 1) options. A 28-power attacker blocked by 7 creatures gives 1,344,904 options at ~14 ints each, which is 18.8M ints for one decision. The new decks make that reachable (Elves' wide boards and Timberwatch pumps, Atog, Tron fatties). A diagnostic sweep over the 15 r6 pairings with random agents found assign_damage as the largest decision in every pairing (up to 1,716 options in elves_tron); every other decision kind stays under ~3k ints.

A bigger slot wouldn't help: a 1.3M-option row would also pad the server's batch shapes and the PPO minibatch to absurd sizes. So the decision has to be bounded where it's created.

## Changes
- **Engine (Python + Rust, identical):** `_damage_splits` / `damage_splits`. Up to `MAX_DAMAGE_SPLITS = 1024` divisions, every division is offered as before. Past that, the decision offers the *lethal splits*: for each subset of the first 10 blockers whose lethal damage fits, exactly lethal to each of them, and the rest to the player (trample, every blocker lethal) or else to the first chosen blocker. Deduplicated, at most 1024 options.
- **Inference client:** a request larger than its slot is split into chunks that fit. They go out one after another on the same slot and `collect` joins the replies. Only a single decision larger than the slot raises, and the message names its options and sizes.

## Behaviour change
This is a rules-engine change, but only for decisions that had more than 1024 damage divisions. Golden digests, `test_difftest` and `test_fuzz` pass without re-recording, so no golden or fuzz game reaches the cap. No expected values in existing tests changed.

## Tests
- `test_rules.py::test_damage_division_past_the_cap_offers_the_lethal_splits` (both engines): a 20-power trampler blocked by seven 1/1s has 888k divisions and now gets 127 lethal splits. Checks the labels and damage.
- `test_inference.py::test_oversized_request_is_split_into_chunks`: 40 decisions through a slot of twice the largest one (5+ chunks) give the same greedy actions and values as a slot that holds them all. A single oversized decision raises a clear error, and the slot keeps working afterwards.
- Ran locally: test_rules, test_golden, test_difftest, test_fuzz, test_inference, test_rollout_stream (242 passed, 6 skipped); ruff clean.

head: 0824f9368e64fbed073723f835e0316839ab7c7e
title: Sacrifice costs: tap the sacrificed permanent for mana first (CR 601.2g-h)
body:
## What

A playtest reported that sacrifice costs are chosen before mana is paid, so an Affinity player cannot tap an artifact land and then sacrifice it to the same cost.

That part was already right in both engines. `_cast` / `_activate` pay mana first and choose the sacrifice after. `_cost_feasible` counts tapped permanents as sacrifice candidates (only self-sacrificing sources such as Spawn or Treasure are removed). So Fanatical Offering paid with Vault of Whispers + Swamp, sacrificing the Vault, already worked.

The real gap: there was no way to get mana from the permanent being sacrificed when that mana is **not** needed for this cost. Mana abilities may be activated before costs are paid (CR 601.2g-h), and the mana floats. Examples:
- Krark-Clan Shaman: tap Great Furnace for R, sacrifice it, cast Galvanic Blast with the R
- Lava Dart flashback: tap the Mountain for R, sacrifice it, Bolt with the R
- Fireblast: tap the Mountains first
- An artifact land's mana before Fanatical Offering or Reckoner's Bargain sacrifices it

## Change

`Game._choose_sacrifice` / `choose_sacrifice` (Rust) now offers `Tap X#id for C, then sacrifice it` for every untapped candidate with a plain tap mana ability, after the plain sacrifice options. Key: `("sacrifice", name, "tap", C)`. Value: `("source", card, C)` / `Val::Source`. Self-sacrificing mana sources are left out. The mana (`mana_amount` units) goes to the pool, then the permanent is sacrificed. This covers every sacrifice **cost**: additional costs, `sac_other` abilities, flashback/alternative land sacrifices. Edicts and Highway Robbery resolve without a payment window, so they are unchanged.

Payability checks need no change: the new options only add mana.

Scripted bots: `score_sacrifice` takes the float option (+0.01 over the plain sacrifice of the same card).

## Tests

- New tests in `test_cards_affinity` (KCS + Great Furnace into Galvanic Blast; tapped / mana-less candidates offer only the plain sacrifice; Fanatical Offering paid with the Vault it sacrifices) and `test_cards_red` (Lava Dart flashback: tap Mountain, then Bolt with the floating R).
- **Test changes alter expected behaviour:** Lava Dart flashback and KCS deathtouch relied on a single sacrifice option being auto-chosen. Now they choose explicitly. The Fireblast and Crop Rotation option-list assertions now include the new tap-then-sacrifice options.
- **Golden digests re-recorded** (`make golden`): test changes alter expected behaviour. The digests were re-recorded because sacrifice costs now also offer tapping the sacrificed permanent for mana first. Mana itself was already paid before the sacrifice was chosen. The decision lists change, so 86 of 210 games diverge.
- **Feature-set digests re-recorded** (`features_v1/v3/v4/v5_digests.json`). They hash random-play games on the pinned decks (`feature_decks.json`). This branch does not touch the featurizer; only the games changed. Games without such a sacrifice keep their old digests (e.g. 15 of 24 in v1). `feature_fixtures.json` is unaffected.

title: Set up isolated Conductor workspaces and shared agent context
body:
Fresh Conductor workspaces lacked an isolated Python/native environment and a discoverable entry point for the project rules. Review prompts also described feature sets 2–3 and assumed no entity attention, even for newer checkpoints.

Add per-workspace setup and Make targets, shared Conductor commands using allocated ports, an AGENTS.md bridge to CLAUDE.md, a curated context index, and a Codex game-review skill using the existing prompt/file tools. Record structured checkpoint configs and build setup-review sheets from each policy's actual feature version and architecture; legacy recordings explicitly report unknown configuration. Claude's Workflow runner and launch configuration remain available.

Validation:
- Fresh `make setup` and repeat setup passed; both project and native imports resolve to this checkout/environment.
- 19 review tests passed, including versions 1–6, legacy files, per-seat prompt configuration and named file replies.
- 79 RL, replay, live-play, entity-attention and inference tests passed (5 skipped, 3 slow/GPU tests deselected) in the fresh environment.
- Ruff, shell syntax, TOML parsing, skill validation and diff whitespace checks passed.
- Replay/live HTTP and UI smoke checks passed concurrently on allocated ports 55000/55001.
- Ten Elves-versus-Tron differential games matched across Python and Rust.

No engine behavior, feature encodings or golden digests changed. The Mac app loads shared Conductor settings from the remote default branch after merge; terminal Make commands work immediately. Keep this PR draft until the user confirms readiness, per CLAUDE.md.

head: 5b1214c8f67b36ae2946a7f5f4a8c75ba07093ef
title: Play against a checkpoint in the web viewer
body:
First step of hosting the viewer for friends: live play against a checkpoint on localhost. Multi-user hardening, Docker and the Cloudflare Tunnel come in later PRs.

## What it does
`python -m mtg_ml.replay serve --models runs/` adds a **Play vs model…** button. You pick a checkpoint (by name, from the `--models` directory), the matchup, your seat, and whether the model samples or plays greedy. Then you play in the browser:
- your options appear in the side panel; click one or press 1–9
- if you play seat 1, the board is flipped so you are at the bottom
- the model's moves are played back one by one (key moments, at the playback speed) before your options unlock, with a link to skip
- reloading the page reconnects to the running game
- the timeline and log let you look back at earlier decisions during the game
- when the game ends, it is saved to `replays/` as an ordinary replay (both hands, the model's policy and value), and **Watch full replay** opens it

## Hidden information
The server holds the game (`mtg_ml/live.py`), and the browser only gets the player's view (`replay.snapshot(..., viewer=seat)`):
- **Model's hand:** face down, with placeholder uids, because real uids follow decklist order and would give the card away. Cards you know (revealed, or put back by Deem Inferior) are shown.
- **Library tops:** only the ones the player knows.
- **Log:** the engine echoes every decision of both players, including private ones (scry, put-backs, mulligan bottoms). The opponent's echoes are dropped; their public actions have log lines of their own.
- **Model's policy and value:** never sent during the game.
- **Model's moves:** each one becomes a frame, but the chosen option is shown only for decision kinds whose choice is public (`rl.features.PUBLIC_KINDS`, the same rule the model's own memory uses). Scry, put-backs and other private choices show only their kind.

## Safety and threading
- **Checkpoints by name only.** The browser chooses a checkpoint by name, never by path, because loading a checkpoint unpickles it and can run code.
- **One worker thread for all games.** Native `PyGame` objects are `unsendable` (they may only be touched by the thread that created them), and `ThreadingHTTPServer` answers each request on a new thread. The first browser test crashed exactly this way. All games now run on one worker thread, and garbage collection after dropping games also happens there.
- **Limits.** At most 8 games at once (the oldest idle one makes room), and idle games expire after 1 h. Requests are limited to 64 KB, and stale or repeated clicks are refused, since each choice carries its frame number.

## Tests
New `tests/test_live.py`:
- **Hidden information:** the opponent's hand and decision echoes never reach the view.
- **Full games:** played to the end for both seats, saved replays checked.
- **Bad requests:** path-like model names, invalid seats, double clicks and out-of-range options are refused.
- **Eviction:** the oldest game makes room when the limit is reached.
- **HTTP end to end on both engines:** a regression test for the threading bug.

Results:
- `make test-fast`: 717 passed (with a freshly built native engine).
- `make lint`: clean.
- Manual browser check with `v3-entity-500k` on the native engine: a full 25-turn game as Mono Blue. The model's hand stayed hidden, apart from a card that Deem Inferior had shown. There were no server errors, and the full replay opened afterwards.

No engine changes, so golden digests and the difftest are untouched.

## Next (later PRs)
- Game ownership by user email (Cloudflare Access JWT) and limits per user
- Persisting games as seed + choice list, so a restart doesn't lose them
- Moving to Starlette/uvicorn
- Docker image (native engine + CPU torch), Hetzner VPS, Cloudflare Tunnel + Access

title: Play against a checkpoint in the web viewer
body:
First step of hosting the viewer for friends: live play against a checkpoint on localhost. Multi-user hardening, Docker and the Cloudflare Tunnel come in later PRs.

## What it does
`python -m mtg_ml.replay serve --models runs/` adds a **Play vs model…** button. You pick a checkpoint (by name, from the `--models` directory), the matchup, your seat, and whether the model samples or plays greedy. Then you play in the browser:
- your options appear in the side panel; click one or press 1–9
- if you play seat 1, the board is flipped so you are at the bottom
- the model's moves are played back one by one (key moments, at the playback speed) before your options unlock, with a link to skip
- reloading the page reconnects to the running game
- the timeline and log let you look back at earlier decisions during the game
- when the game ends, it is saved to `replays/` as an ordinary replay (both hands, the model's policy and value), and **Watch full replay** opens it

## Hidden information
The server holds the game (`mtg_ml/live.py`), and the browser only gets the player's view (`replay.snapshot(..., viewer=seat)`):
- **Model's hand:** face down, with placeholder uids, because real uids follow decklist order and would give the card away. Cards you know (revealed, or put back by Deem Inferior) are shown.
- **Library tops:** only the ones the player knows.
- **Log:** the engine echoes every decision of both players, including private ones (scry, put-backs, mulligan bottoms). The opponent's echoes are dropped; their public actions have log lines of their own.
- **Model's policy and value:** never sent during the game.
- **Model's moves:** each one becomes a frame, but the chosen option is shown only for decision kinds whose choice is public (`rl.features.PUBLIC_KINDS`, the same rule the model's own memory uses). Scry, put-backs and other private choices show only their kind.

## Safety and threading
- **Checkpoints by name only.** The browser chooses a checkpoint by name, never by path, because loading a checkpoint unpickles it and can run code.
- **One worker thread for all games.** Native `PyGame` objects are `unsendable` (they may only be touched by the thread that created them), and `ThreadingHTTPServer` answers each request on a new thread. The first browser test crashed exactly this way. All games now run on one worker thread, and garbage collection after dropping games also happens there.
- **Limits.** At most 8 games at once (the oldest idle one makes room), and idle games expire after 1 h. Requests are limited to 64 KB, and stale or repeated clicks are refused, since each choice carries its frame number.

## Tests
New `tests/test_live.py`:
- **Hidden information:** the opponent's hand and decision echoes never reach the view.
- **Full games:** played to the end for both seats, saved replays checked.
- **Bad requests:** path-like model names, invalid seats, double clicks and out-of-range options are refused.
- **Eviction:** the oldest game makes room when the limit is reached.
- **HTTP end to end on both engines:** a regression test for the threading bug.

Results:
- `make test-fast`: 717 passed (with a freshly built native engine).
- `make lint`: clean.
- Manual browser check with `v3-entity-500k` on the native engine: a full 25-turn game as Mono Blue. The model's hand stayed hidden, apart from a card that Deem Inferior had shown. There were no server errors, and the full replay opened afterwards.

No engine changes, so golden digests and the difftest are untouched.

- Game ownership by user email (Cloudflare Access JWT) and limits per user
- Persisting games as seed + choice list, so a restart doesn't lose them
- Moving to Starlette/uvicorn
- Docker image (native engine + CPU torch), Hetzner VPS, Cloudflare Tunnel + Access
